Senses.Explanation: The lion appears through cubs, roars, and full-force capture in the stored Chan encounters. A lion. Chan records repeatedly deploy the animal in lineage and speech vocabulary: a capable successor is a 'lion cub' and forceful proclamation is a 'lion's roar.' The Blue Cliff Record pairs an outstanding, keen fellow with a lion cub; Zhaozhou is called a true lion cub, well able to roar. A recorded old adept says that a lion uses its complete strength for both rabbit and elephant, then names that strength the strength that does not deceive. Another inherited formula contrasts proclamation with attainment, calling teaching with something obtained a jackal's cry and teaching without something obtained a lion's roar. These are explicit corpus uses; the entry assigns no hidden animal symbolism.

Senses.Explanation: A lion cub is a young lion. Chan records repeatedly bend this animal image into a public test-name and appraisal for a person. Mazu asks a lecturer who boasts of expounding many texts, “are you not a lion cub?”; after the lecturer declines the name, Mazu makes a hissing sound and the exchange continues. Named teachers say “a true lion cub, well able to roar” (真師子兒，善能哮吼) after a reviewed unnamed participant shouts or answers; in one lineage narrative this appraisal is followed by entering the chamber and receiving the seal. A direct question, “what is the lion cub?” receives “the tips of its hair line up the cosmos” (毛頭排宇宙). Formal verse places the cub in the lion's cave roaring until heaven and earth split, while another warning says that a true lion cub does not eat leftover soup. Later commentary can sharpen or contest an appraisal, saying that when Dongyuan opened his mouth to roar his fathers and ancestors were already lost. The Zen-specific bend is the recurrent use of the young lion as an explicit name given, refused, tested, and confirmed in encounters, often by the observable ability to roar. The entry does not infer succession whenever the words occur.

Senses.Explanation: The lion’s roar is explicitly defined against the jackal’s cry as teaching without something gained, and later records demand, test, or appraise that roar in public exchange. In the Chan record it names forceful speech or teaching and is repeatedly opposed to the cry of a jackal. One record supplies an explicit definition: ‘teaching with something gained is the jackal's cry; teaching with nothing gained is called the lion's roar’ (說法有所得，斯則野干鳴；說法無所得，是名師子吼). The phrase is not merely an appraisal applied by compilers: Baozi Guangyun tells his interlocutor to ‘try making a lion's roar,’ and monks claim it, and it becomes a public-interview challenge. Guishan says that Shishuang's speaking of Chan is ‘like a lion's roar, frightening the foxes, wolves, and jackals to death.’ In another exchange an unnamed monastic asks what happens on meeting a lion's roar; Shoushan Xingnian answers ‘let the jackal cry as it likes,’ after which the unnamed monastic shouts. Thus an animal sound is bent into a name, test, and verdict for speech in the teaching encounter; the texts themselves establish the lion/jackal contrast without requiring an imported symbolic reading.

Senses.Explanation: This is the final formidable barrier or severe checkpoint in a sequence of testing, something speakers say must be reached, passed through, or personally arrived at even after an earlier understanding. ‘Final’ marks its position and (牢) marks its formidable resistance; neither word by itself supplies the whole expression. The records speak of passing through or penetrating it, and use it as a severe last check. Yuan'an, after listing a series of named cases, calls "this whole tangle" (者一落索) the final locked barrier and criticizes estimating it through cognitive calculation. Juelang says even someone who has understood "this affair" but has "not passed through the final locked barrier" (未透末後牢關) can still mistake a shadow for a head. Yulin asks, "how many people have passed the final locked barrier?" (末後牢關幾人透得). Other formulations say it is "not measurable by humans or gods" (人天莫測) and "not understood by a thousand sages" (千聖不曉).

Senses.Explanation: Dafang Xinghai's mountain verse is the corpus's direct plant action: he is too indolent to gather purple fungus beside the stream (懶去溪邊採紫芝). The plant-name circulates much more widely in the compound Purple Fungus Song. Tiantong Shanxin is publicly asked what that song is and answers by clapping; Fahua Quanju answers an independent transmission of the question by saying that it is not a Wu sound but must be Han speech (不是吳音，切湏漢語). Yongjue Yuanxian asks who will join a solitary recluse in singing it (中有幽人守貞獨，誰來同唱紫芝歌), Xisou Shaotan places groups of two and three singing it on stones under pine roots (三三兩兩松根石上唱紫芝歌), and Yuanwu Keqin asks who can sing it in the season of high mountains, autumn wind, and a single goose (誰當此時節，解唱紫芝歌). Wuwen Daocan separately invokes the Four Hoaryheads of Mount Shang and their heart of withdrawal, but his verse does not contain the headword. Zen bends the plant-name into a song asked about in public interviews and sung in mountain-retreat verse. The evidence does not make the bare word itself the title of a second thing.

Senses.Explanation: Through-and-through. Shangfeng Bencai's formula contrasts the relative ease of emerging from one's situation with the difficulty of speaking through-and-through. Feiyin Tongrong applies the same force to conduct after former valuables have been dropped, and Yinyuan Longqi to taking the matter up completely. Chaozong Tongren joins the term to completion, Yushan Shangsi to accord, Guishan Zhe to departing free, and Miyun Yuanwu to full disclosure. The changing predicates preserve one intensifying job rather than seven separate things. Zen bends a bodily image into a demand with no protected remainder. The corpus tests whether speech, accord, responsibility, or manifestation is complete in the whole person, not merely asserted in part.

Senses.Explanation: To be blankly at a loss. In Chan encounter narratives it is an observable failure to answer or proceed: after being asked "who observes, and what is quiet?" the recorded questioner is at a loss; after being seized and ordered "speak! speak!" the recorded questioner is at a loss and is pushed away. The record makes the absence of an answer explicit in "the narrator records that Wenshu Zhengdao was at a loss and did not know how to reply" (師茫然不知對). It also applies collectively: after the answer "clear conversation face to face—if not buddha, then who?" the assembly is all at a loss (眾皆茫然). A training biography records a student being required to give one fitting word and withdrawing at a loss (師茫然退). The Zen deviation lies in this recurring public-interview function: the adjective marks the recorded point where a participant or assembly has no response, not a mystical state and not an explanation of why the exchange defeated them.
